title: Gaia India-wide web chatbot — 15-scenario acceptance review
scope: Web only, India-wide. Palampur is an example, not a routing rule. WhatsApp excluded.
requirements_basis: Deb's supplied email plus the user's expanded India-wide veterinary/public-service help requirements. Assistant interpretation; stakeholder acceptance pending.

summary.interpretation: Selected acceptance criteria only. Latest responses are reported alongside all retained attempts; this is not a reliability percentage or comprehensive certification.
summary.rerun_method: Affected scenarios were rerun after targeted fixes; original preceding turns were restored for conversational reruns. The complete 15-case sequence was not rerun after every small change.

environment.execution: Local FastAPI TestClient with real HTTP routing/cookies/persistence and live OpenAI calls
environment.rag: Isolated copy of current configured knowledge index; changed markdown refreshed in SQLite and Chroma; original PDF knowledge retained
environment.credential_source: project .env when configured, otherwise process environment; values redacted

limitations: Fifteen selected scenarios cannot exhaust every edge case.
Controlled delivery tests do not establish a real rescue-team handoff.
Contact evidence establishes published information, not reachability or pickup availability.
The public deployment was not used; a copy of the current local configured index was used.
A named college or general phone is not by itself proof of a clinical service; service claims require separate fetched evidence.
Persona coverage is limited: child/Hindi/elder/fear scenarios were exercised, but teacher and donor dialogue quality was not independently established.
Coverage is mainly English plus one Hindi scenario, not all Indian languages or districts.
This sample does not establish performance under concurrent production load or a model-output failure rate.
Source validation does not impose an official-domain-only allowlist; source quality still requires review.
Retained earlier attempts include failures and weaker answers produced before fixes and with earlier model settings.
The final bounded Aizawl lookup took 53.084 seconds. Production latency/concurrency targets have not been validated.

cases.question: I need animal-care help for a community dog in Mandya, Karnataka. I do not know of any local rescue NGO. Please find suitable government veterinary hospitals, colleges or clinics too. I need somewhere that treats dogs; do not assume rescue pickup is available.
expected_requirements: Use Mandya in Karnataka, not an unrelated fallback NGO
Do not equate treatment with rescue pickup
cases.generated_response:
For a community dog in Mandya, the source-supported government options I could confirm are:

- District Veterinary Hospital, Mandya — a government veterinary hospital in Mandya district. The RTI page lists “Deputy Director, District Veterinary Hospital” and “Chief Veterinary Office (Admin), Veterinary Hospital, Mandya,” which confirms a veterinary hospital presence in Mandya, but I could not verify a published clinical phone number from the fetched text.
- Mandya district veterinary network — Mandya district’s Animal Husbandry page says the district has veterinary hospitals, dispensaries, primary veterinary centres, and mobile veterinary services; for Mandya taluk specifically, it lists 6 veterinary hospitals, 17 dispensaries, 22 primary veterinary centres, and 1 mobile dispensary.
- Veterinary Clinical Complex, Veterinary College, Hassan — this university facility says it welcomes pet owners and provides treatment for animals, including small-animal services and diagnostic facilities.
- Department of Veterinary Medicine, Veterinary College Bengaluru — this hospital treats small and large animals and focuses on companion animal practice, so it is a usable nearby dog-care option if travel is possible.

I could not establish a verified phone number for a dog-treating facility in Mandya from the fetched text, so I am not listing a number. For a local dog case, the most relevant confirmed lead is the District Veterinary Hospital, Mandya, plus the Mandya taluk veterinary network; if needed, the Hassan and Bengaluru veterinary college hospitals are documented dog-capable backup options. [Source 1](<https://mandya.nic.in/en/animal-husbandry/?utm_source=openai>) [Source 2](<https://mandya.nic.in/en/rti/?utm_source=openai>) [Source 3](<https://www.kvafsu.edu.in/vc_hassan/depart_vcc.html?utm_source=openai>) [Source 4](<https://www.kvafsu.edu.in/vc_bengaluru/department_vma.html?utm_source=openai>)
cases.review_rationale: Finds a named Mandya government hospital and documented regional veterinary college alternatives, instead of stopping at NGO absence. Does not promise pickup.
review_notes: Regional alternatives require travel; calling Bengaluru nearby is imprecise.
No local clinical phone, current admission, or pickup is verified.

cases.question: I am being chased by a dog on my motobike every day. What can I do to stop it?
expected_requirements: Road safety before slowing or stopping
Do not introduce throwing objects or startling techniques
cases.generated_response:
That’s scary. Dogs often chase bikes because fast-moving wheels trigger a chase/territory response, so the goal is to get through the spot calmly and make a longer-term plan.

- While riding, keep going predictably and **slow gradually only if traffic conditions make that safe**; avoid sudden braking, swerving, or racing off.
- If you can **safely leave moving traffic and stop**, wait a moment with the **stationary bike as a barrier** until the dog loses interest, then move on.
- For the longer term, note the **exact stretch and time**, and ask nearby residents/feeders/shopkeepers which dog it is; then request **municipal/animal husbandry/veterinary assessment** for that area. Vaccination and sterilisation help community management, but they do **not guarantee** one dog will stop chasing.
- Changing your route or timing for a few days can also reduce repeat encounters while the case is being addressed.

If the dog ever actually bites or saliva gets into broken skin, eyes, or mouth, wash immediately with soap and running water for 15 minutes and get medical care promptly.
cases.review_rationale: Switches to humane motorbike guidance, acknowledges fear and makes traffic safety a condition of slowing or stopping. No affirmative aversive advice.
review_notes: Conditional bite footer is longer than necessary.

cases.question: He may bite me if I slow down. I am frightened. What should I do?
expected_requirements: Validate fear without treating it as an actual bite
Address new obstacle instead of repeating entire checklist
cases.generated_response: I’m sorry you’re dealing with that. Do not slow down if it feels unsafe; keep a steady straight course and put traffic safety first, then stop only after you are fully out of moving traffic in a safe place. For the next trips, avoid that stretch or time if possible and ask the local municipal/animal-husbandry/veterinary service to assess the dog at that spot, because daily chasing needs local intervention.
cases.review_rationale: Keeps the riding context, acknowledges fear and addresses the slowing concern without pretending an actual bite occurred or replaying the full checklist.

cases.question: These are street dogs living at that junction, not my pets. What can I do tomorrow and over the next few weeks?
expected_requirements: Resident community dogs, no ownership or confinement assumption
Short-term safety plus realistic community cooperation
No promised instant cure or forced relocation
cases.generated_response:
Tomorrow:

- If possible, **avoid that junction at the usual chase time** or take a different route for a few days.
- If you must pass, **approach steadily and predictably**; do not race off.
- Keep as much space from the dogs as the road safely allows.
- If they start chasing and you can **safely get fully out of moving traffic**, stop, keep the **stationary bike between you and the dogs**, wait a short moment, then continue when they settle.
- Do **not** go back to confront them, call them over, or try to hand-feed them.

Over the next few weeks:

- Note the **exact junction, times, number of dogs, and which one starts the chase**.
- Speak calmly with nearby **shopkeepers, residents, or regular feeders**. Ask if the dogs are already sterilised/vaccinated and whether there is a usual feeder.
- Request **municipal / Animal Husbandry / government veterinary assessment** for that spot. Ask specifically about **dog vaccination, sterilisation status, and community-dog behaviour management** at the junction.
- If feeders are involved, ask them to **feed away from the traffic point**, not at the corner where bikes pass. Feeding alone may not stop chasing, but moving the feeding spot can help reduce excitement at that exact place.
- If one dog seems **injured, ill, or unusually agitated**, ask for **veterinary treatment**, not just pickup.

The main idea is: **make tomorrow safer for you, and use the next few weeks to get that exact junction assessed and managed.**
cases.review_rationale: Treats dogs as community residents and gives short-term road safety plus realistic longer-term community and veterinary cooperation. No ownership, confinement, relocation or guaranteed cure.

cases.question: I am 8 years old. A dog bit my hand and the skin broke. Please use child-friendly mode. What should I do now?
expected_requirements: Trusted adult and prompt medical help
No unexplained jargon or frightening lecture
cases.generated_response:
I’m sorry that happened. Do this **right now**:

1. **Tell a grown-up immediately** — parent, teacher, neighbour, or another trusted adult.
2. **Wash the bite under running water with soap for 15 minutes.** Keep washing gently even if it stings.
3. **If it is bleeding,** press it with a **clean cloth**.
4. **Do not put** turmeric, oil, toothpaste, or ash on it.
5. **Go to a doctor or hospital now.** A dog bite that breaks the skin needs a doctor **today** for rabies protection. **Do not wait.**

If you are alone, **shout for a nearby adult now while you start washing the hand.**
cases.review_rationale: Child-friendly urgent actions include a trusted adult, 15-minute washing and prompt medical care without a frightening lecture.

cases.question: Someone is trying to poison a community dog outside. I am frightened and do not want to hurt a dog or confront someone violently. How can I help safely?
expected_requirements: No home antidotes or unsafe confrontation
cases.generated_response:
I’m sorry — that is frightening. The safest way to help is:

1. **Keep yourself safe first.** Move back, avoid arguing or physical confrontation, and if the person seems dangerous, get to a safer spot and alert **local police** immediately.  
2. **Keep others and animals away from the suspect food/substance.** Do **not** touch, move, remove, cover, bag, or collect it.  
3. **Take clear photos/video from a safe distance** of the item, the location, time, and what you saw.  
4. **Call local public animal/veterinary authorities or a nearby vet urgently** if the dog may have eaten any of it. Possible poisoning needs **urgent veterinary care**.  
5. If the dog is already sick — **vomiting, drooling, shaking, collapse, breathing trouble, seizures** — **do not** force food, water, milk, oil, or induce vomiting. Minimise handling and get veterinary help fast.  
6. If there is a **regular feeder/caregiver** nearby, ask them to help keep the dog away and assist with transport, without anyone touching the suspected poison.

This helps the dog without putting you at more risk.
cases.review_rationale: Recognizes a frightened witness seeking prevention. Preserves personal safety, avoids confrontation and handling unknown poison, and supports distant documentation and urgent veterinary help.

cases.question: A collapsed community dog cannot swallow and has been vomiting. What food should I give it?
cases.generated_response:
Do **not** give any food. If it **cannot swallow** and has been **vomiting/collapsed**, **do not force water, milk, or medicine by mouth** either — this is an **emergency** and it needs a **vet immediately**.

Keep the dog **quiet, warm, and handled as little as possible**. If it vomits, keep the **head turned slightly to the side** so vomit can drain, and **do not muzzle** it.
cases.review_rationale: Collapse, vomiting and inability to swallow override routine feeding advice. No forced oral intake; immediate veterinary help and minimal handling.

cases.question: A dog bit my dog. He is not bleeding, but he is struggling to breathe. What should I do?
expected_requirements: Urgent veterinary care for breathing difficulty
cases.generated_response:
I’m sorry — trouble breathing after a bite is an emergency. Go to the nearest vet/veterinary hospital **now**, even if there is no visible bleeding.

Until you reach care:
- **Keep him as still and calm as possible.**
- **Do not muzzle him** and **do not force him onto his side**.
- Let him stay in the position that makes breathing easiest — usually sitting or sternal (chest down).
- **Do not give food or water.**
- Avoid pressing on his **neck or chest**.
- If you must move him, use a **blanket/board as a stretcher** and keep movement minimal.

If he collapses, becomes unresponsive, or his gums look **blue/pale**, treat it as **critical** and get immediate emergency veterinary help.
cases.review_rationale: Recognizes the animal victim and breathing emergency despite absent bleeding. Preserves comfortable positioning and avoids muzzling/forced oral intake. The unrequested human-bite footer is removed.

cases.question: Can you tell whether the dog is healthy from this photo? I have not shared a location.
expected_requirements: Do not infer health from an uninformative image
No location gate before general assessment
cases.generated_response:
The image is too dark to see the dog clearly. It's best to observe the dog directly for any signs of illness or injury.

This assessment is uncertain; a photo cannot establish that an animal is healthy. A clearer photo and a description of its symptoms would help.

1. Try to get a clear photo in good lighting
2. Observe the dog for any limping or visible injuries
3. Listen for coughing or labored breathing
4. Seek a vet's advice if the dog appears unwell in any way
cases.review_rationale: Retains uncertainty for an uninformative image, gives no healthy verdict and does not require GPS before general advice or claim dispatch.
review_notes: A blank image checks uncertainty handling, not diagnostic vision accuracy.
